topic: Use of amount of substance in relation to volumes of gases (chemistry only) (HT only)
subject: chemistry

items.q: A flask holds 2.0 g of hydrogen gas, H2 (Mr = 2). Which sample of oxygen gas, O2 (Mr = 32), occupies the same volume at the same temperature and pressure?
items.why: Mass is the quantity students actually measure on a balance, so it feels like the real amount of stuff. The specification statement is about amounts in moles, but 'amount' is read as an everyday word meaning 'how much', which students equate with mass. Read the statement literally: equal amounts in moles. Convert each mass to moles with mass ÷ relative formula mass before comparing anything. Only when the mole figures match will the volumes match.

items.q: Two identical sealed flasks are at the same temperature and pressure. One contains nitrogen, N2 (Mr = 28), and the other contains methane, CH4 (Mr = 16). Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Both flasks hold the same amount in moles of gas
items.misconception: Both flasks hold the same mass of gas in grams
items.why: Mass is the quantity students actually measure on a balance, so it feels like the real amount of stuff. The specification statement is about amounts in moles, but 'amount' is read as an everyday word meaning 'how much', which students equate with mass. Read the statement literally: equal amounts in moles. Convert each mass to moles with mass ÷ relative formula mass before comparing anything. Only when the mole figures match will the volumes match.
items.random_wrong: The nitrogen flask holds more moles because N2 is heavier

items.q: What is the volume of one mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure?
items.why: Students meet 25 °C as the standard temperature quoted for enthalpy and solubility data, and 0 °C with 22.4 dm³ from textbooks and websites that use standard temperature and pressure. Both get filed under the same vague heading of 'normal conditions'. Learn the pair together: RTP is 20 °C and 1 atmosphere, and the molar volume that goes with it is 24 dm³. If a source quotes 22.4 dm³, it is using different conditions from the ones this specification sets.

items.q: Room temperature and pressure, the conditions at which one mole of gas occupies 24 dm³, means:
items.why: Students meet 25 °C as the standard temperature quoted for enthalpy and solubility data, and 0 °C with 22.4 dm³ from textbooks and websites that use standard temperature and pressure. Both get filed under the same vague heading of 'normal conditions'. Learn the pair together: RTP is 20 °C and 1 atmosphere, and the molar volume that goes with it is 24 dm³. If a source quotes 22.4 dm³, it is using different conditions from the ones this specification sets.

items.q: What volume does 8.8 g of carbon dioxide, CO2 (Mr = 44), occupy at room temperature and pressure?
items.why: The molar volume is remembered as 'times 24' rather than as 'dm³ per mole', so the ÷ Mr step drops out whenever the question hands over a mass instead of a mole figure. Write the units on the 24: it is 24 dm³ per mole, so it can only multiply a number of moles. If your figure is in grams, divide by the relative formula mass first.

items.q: A balloon contains 1.2 dm³ of methane, CH4 (Mr = 16), at room temperature and pressure. What is the mass of methane in the balloon?
items.why: Rearranging is learnt as a pattern of moving symbols around a triangle rather than as doing the same operation to both sides, so an inverted fraction looks just as plausible as the right one. Do the inverse operation to both sides, then test the result with easy numbers: 1 mol must give 24 dm³. Put 24 dm³ into your rearranged formula and check it returns 1 mol.

items.q: Ammonia is made by the reaction N2(g) + 3H2(g) → 2NH3(g). 20 cm³ of nitrogen reacts completely with excess hydrogen. What volume of ammonia forms, measured at the same temperature and pressure?
items.why: Conservation of mass is drilled hard, and students extend it to volume because both feel like measures of 'how much'. The idea is reinforced by liquid reactions where volume changes are not noticed. Only mass is conserved, not the volume of gas. Count moles of gas on each side using the balancing numbers; if that total changes, the total gas volume changes with it.

items.q: Carbon monoxide burns as follows: 2CO(g) + O2(g) → 2CO2(g). What volume of oxygen reacts exactly with 100 cm³ of carbon monoxide, all volumes measured at the same temperature and pressure?
items.why: Conservation of mass is drilled hard, and students extend it to volume because both feel like measures of 'how much'. The idea is reinforced by liquid reactions where volume changes are not noticed. Only mass is conserved, not the volume of gas. Count moles of gas on each side using the balancing numbers; if that total changes, the total gas volume changes with it.

items.q: In the reaction 2CO(g) + O2(g) → 2CO2(g), 100 cm³ of carbon monoxide reacts completely with 50 cm³ of oxygen at RTP. Which statement about the total volume of gas is correct?
items.correct: It falls to 100 cm³: three volumes give two
items.misconception: It stays at 150 cm³ because mass is conserved
items.why: Conservation of mass is drilled hard, and students extend it to volume because both feel like measures of 'how much'. The idea is reinforced by liquid reactions where volume changes are not noticed. Only mass is conserved, not the volume of gas. Count moles of gas on each side using the balancing numbers; if that total changes, the total gas volume changes with it.
items.random_wrong: It rises to 200 cm³ because CO2 has a larger Mr

items.q: Calcium carbonate decomposes: CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g). 50 g of calcium carbonate (Mr = 100) decomposes completely. What volume of gas is produced at room temperature and pressure?
items.why: The rule is remembered as 'one mole occupies 24 dm³' with the word 'gas' dropped, and state symbols are often skimmed over as decoration rather than read as data the calculation depends on. Read the state symbols before doing anything. Ring the gases in the equation and use only those balancing numbers in the volume ratio; solids and liquids occupy a negligible volume by comparison.

items.q: Methane burns completely: CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(l). 40 cm³ of methane is burned in excess oxygen. What is the total volume of gaseous product at RTP, measured at the same temperature and pressure as the methane?
items.why: The rule is remembered as 'one mole occupies 24 dm³' with the word 'gas' dropped, and state symbols are often skimmed over as decoration rather than read as data the calculation depends on. Read the state symbols before doing anything. Ring the gases in the equation and use only those balancing numbers in the volume ratio; solids and liquids occupy a negligible volume by comparison.

items.q: Propane burns completely: C3H8(g) + 5O2(g) → 3CO2(g) + 4H2O(l). What volume of oxygen is needed to burn 25 cm³ of propane completely, both volumes measured at the same temperature and pressure?
items.why: Rearranging is learnt as a pattern of moving symbols around a triangle rather than as doing the same operation to both sides, so an inverted fraction looks just as plausible as the right one. Do the inverse operation to both sides, then test the result with easy numbers: 1 mol must give 24 dm³. Put 24 dm³ into your rearranged formula and check it returns 1 mol.

items.q: The volume V in dm³ of a mass m grams of a gas at RTP is given by V = (m ÷ Mr) × 24. Which rearrangement makes Mr the subject?
items.why: Rearranging is learnt as a pattern of moving symbols around a triangle rather than as doing the same operation to both sides, so an inverted fraction looks just as plausible as the right one. Do the inverse operation to both sides, then test the result with easy numbers: 1 mol must give 24 dm³. Put 24 dm³ into your rearranged formula and check it returns 1 mol.

items.q: 0.96 g of a gas occupies 720 cm³ at room temperature and pressure. What is the relative formula mass of the gas?
items.why: Students generalise from the linear conversion 1 dm = 10 cm and forget that a volume conversion cubes the factor, giving 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000. Fix 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³ and check the size of the answer: 24 dm³ is 24 000 cm³, roughly the volume of a large box, so a 720 cm³ sample must be a small fraction of a mole.

items.q: Which of these gas samples occupies the greatest volume at room temperature and pressure?
items.why: Mass is the quantity students actually measure on a balance, so it feels like the real amount of stuff. The specification statement is about amounts in moles, but 'amount' is read as an everyday word meaning 'how much', which students equate with mass. Read the statement literally: equal amounts in moles. Convert each mass to moles with mass ÷ relative formula mass before comparing anything. Only when the mole figures match will the volumes match.

items.q: Carbon dioxide molecules are much bigger than hydrogen molecules. Does a mole of carbon dioxide therefore take up more space than a mole of hydrogen?
items.correct: No. At the same temperature and pressure one mole of any gas occupies the same volume, 24 dm³ at room temperature and pressure. The size of the individual molecules does not change the volume of the gas.
items.misconception: Bigger molecules take up more room, so a mole of a gas made of large molecules must fill a bigger container than a mole of a gas made of small ones.
items.why: Students transfer a picture that works for solids and liquids, where the particles are touching and particle size does set the volume, to gases, where the particles are far apart and the space between them dominates. Apply the specification statement as written: equal amounts in moles of gases occupy the same volume under the same conditions. The rule says 'any gas', which rules out molecular size as a factor.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: One mole of gas occupies 24 dm³. Is that true whatever the temperature and pressure?
items.correct: No. The figure of 24 dm³ per mole is given for room temperature and pressure, that is 20 °C and 1 atmosphere pressure. Equal amounts in moles occupy equal volumes only when the gases are under the same conditions of temperature and pressure.
items.misconception: 24 dm³ per mole is a fixed property of gases, like a relative formula mass, so it can be used in any question about a gas.
items.why: The number is met as a constant to be memorised and is used in every calculation students see, so the conditions attached to it fade into background wording that is never tested directly. Say the whole statement, not just the number: one mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³ at room temperature and pressure. Check the stem says RTP before using 24.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the 24 dm³ figure only apply to simple gases such as hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen?
items.correct: No. It applies to any gas. One mole of ammonia, one mole of chlorine and one mole of carbon dioxide each occupy 24 dm³ at room temperature and pressure.
items.misconception: Each gas must have its own molar volume, because each gas has its own relative formula mass and density.
items.why: Every other number students use in mole calculations is substance-specific, so a value that is the same for everything looks suspicious and gets treated as a special case for the gases used in the worked examples. The specification says 'any gas'. Different gases differ in the mass of one mole, not in the volume of one mole; that difference in mass per fixed volume is what makes their densities differ.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Once you know there are 0.05 mol of methane, do you multiply by the relative formula mass to get the volume at RTP?
items.correct: No. Multiplying moles by relative formula mass gives the mass in grams, 0.8 g. To get the volume at RTP you multiply moles by 24, giving 1.2 dm³.
items.misconception: The relative formula mass is what converts a mole figure into a real quantity, so it is used for volumes as well as masses.
items.why: Mass calculations are met first and practised most, so mass ÷ Mr and moles × Mr become the default moves that get applied whenever a mole figure appears, regardless of what the question asks for. Match the conversion to the quantity: × Mr gives grams, × 24 gives dm³ at RTP. Ask what unit the answer needs before choosing which one to use.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In 2CO + O2 → 2CO2, the carbon dioxide molecules are heavier than the carbon monoxide molecules. Does the gas volume therefore increase?
items.correct: No. Three volumes of gas react to give two volumes, so the total gas volume falls. Relative formula mass has no effect on the volume occupied by a given number of moles of gas.
items.misconception: A gas with a bigger relative formula mass takes up more room, so making a heavier product increases the volume.
items.why: Heavier is confused with bigger, and density is remembered as 'heavy things take up more space' rather than as mass per unit volume. Denser gases feel like they should be more spread out. For gases at the same temperature and pressure, only the number of moles sets the volume. A bigger relative formula mass means more mass in the same 24 dm³, which is a greater density, not a greater volume.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do you have to convert gas volumes into masses, using relative formula masses, before you can use the balanced equation?
items.correct: No. For gases at the same temperature and pressure the volumes are in the same ratio as the balancing numbers, so you can work straight from the equation. Relative formula masses are not needed when volume is given and volume is wanted.
items.misconception: The balanced equation only works with masses or moles, so any volume must be turned into a mass with the relative formula mass before the ratio can be applied.
items.why: Reacting-mass calculations are taught first and always route through moles, so students assume every equation calculation must take the same path and treat the direct volume ratio as a shortcut that cannot be trusted. Because one mole of every gas occupies the same volume, moles and volumes are in the same proportion for gases. Apply the balancing numbers to the volumes directly, keeping every volume in the same unit.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In volume = (mass ÷ Mr) × 24, how do you make Mr the subject?
items.correct: Multiply both sides by Mr and divide both sides by volume: Mr = (mass × 24) ÷ volume. For 0.96 g occupying 0.72 dm³, Mr = (0.96 × 24) ÷ 0.72 = 32.
items.misconception: To move a number across the equals sign you change its sign or move it to the other side of the fraction line, so the 24 can be shifted from a multiply to a divide wherever it is convenient.
items.why: Rearranging is treated as relocating symbols rather than as performing the same operation on both sides, so 'take it across and flip it' becomes a rule applied without checking which operation it undoes. Undo one operation at a time on both sides and write each line out. Then substitute a known case to check: 1 mol of a gas with Mr 32 has mass 32 g and volume 24 dm³, and (32 × 24) ÷ 24 = 32.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
